title: Population Pharmacokinetics of Warfarin
text:
NoteEducational scope



This is an independent educational case study developed to build practical experience in population pharmacokinetic modeling with Monolix and R.
The analysis was not designed for clinical decision-making, dose selection, regulatory use, or publication. Results should therefore be interpreted as a demonstration of model-development reasoning rather than as a new clinical model of warfarin.

title: Population Pharmacokinetics of Warfarin
text:
Project overview
I used a publicly available warfarin pharmacokinetic dataset to develop and evaluate a population PK model through a stepwise nonlinear mixed-effects modeling workflow.
The project focused on learning how structural, statistical, and covariate modeling decisions interact. Rather than selecting a model solely from its objective function, I evaluated convergence, parameter precision, diagnostic plots, biological plausibility, and bootstrap stability.
The final model was a parsimonious one-compartment model with delayed first-order absorption, linear elimination, a combined residual-error model, fixed allometric effects of body weight, and an estimated effect of age on clearance.

title: Population Pharmacokinetics of Warfarin
Population Pharmacokinetics of Warfarin
Population Pharmacokinetics of Warfarin
Population Pharmacokinetics of Warfarin
text:
Structural-model investigation
A two-compartment model improved the likelihood-based criteria and produced reasonable individual predictions. However, the apparent improvement was not supported by adequate parameter stability.
In particular, intercompartmental clearance (Q) showed:

a high relative standard error;
strong sensitivity to initialization;
an extremely broad and asymmetric bootstrap distribution;
occasional implausibly large estimates in resampled datasets.

The bootstrap mean for (Q) was strongly influenced by extreme runs and was substantially different from its median and reference estimate. This indicated that the available sampling design did not reliably support estimation of the additional distribution parameters.
For this reason, the two-compartment model was not retained despite its lower objective function.






TipModeling lesson



A more complex model can improve likelihood-based criteria while still being poorly supported by the data. Parameter stability, identifiability, and predictive behavior must be considered together with AIC, BIC, and the objective function.

title: Population Pharmacokinetics of Warfarin
text:
Covariate assessment
Initial diagnostic analyses showed strong relationships between individual volume estimates and body weight and a weaker relationship between clearance and body weight.
Weight effects on volume and clearance were therefore represented through fixed allometric scaling. This reduced the need to estimate poorly supported covariate exponents while retaining a physiologically interpretable relationship.
After accounting for weight, age remained associated with the clearance random effect. An age effect was consequently evaluated and retained in the final educational model.
Sex was investigated but was not retained after accounting for the available continuous covariates.

title: Population Pharmacokinetics of Warfarin
Population Pharmacokinetics of Warfarin
text:
Sampling-design investigation
Inspection of individuals with large standardized clearance effects showed that these estimates were not explained by a single sampling category.
Both richly sampled and late-only participants contributed to the extremes. This suggested that the observed behavior reflected a combination of genuine individual profiles, residual variability, small-sample effects, and limited information rather than a simple data-processing error.
The exercise reinforced the importance of evaluating individual parameter estimates in the context of each subject’s observation schedule.

title: Population Pharmacokinetics of Warfarin
text:
Key lessons
This project provided practical experience with several central principles of population PK model development:

Model complexity must be supported by the data.
A lower objective function did not justify retaining an unstable two-compartment structure.
Covariate selection requires multiple forms of evidence.
Statistical tests, diagnostic plots, biological plausibility, uncertainty, and parameter stability were considered together.
Bootstrap distributions can reveal weaknesses hidden by local standard errors.
The instability of (Q) became especially clear through resampling.
Good individual predictions are not sufficient evidence of model adequacy.
Residual behavior, parameter distributions, predictive diagnostics, and uncertainty must also be examined.
Transparent limitations strengthen an educational analysis.
The final model is useful as a learning exercise while remaining subject to the limitations of a small historical dataset.

title: Endothelial Patterning Through Notch–Dll4 Signaling
text:
Angiogenesis depends on coordinated signaling between neighboring endothelial cells. Through lateral inhibition mediated by the Notch–Dll4 pathway, these cells acquire distinct tip and stalk phenotypes that guide the formation of new blood vessels.
I developed a mechanistic, ordinary differential equation-based model to investigate how endothelial cells communicate and differentiate under different oxygen conditions and levels of VEGFA stimulation.
The model integrates intracellular and intercellular signaling to connect molecular pathway activation with endothelial cell patterning and functional responses.

title: Endothelial Patterning Through Notch–Dll4 Signaling
text:
Angiogenesis depends on coordinated signaling between neighboring endothelial cells. Through lateral inhibition mediated by the Notch–Dll4 pathway, these cells acquire distinct tip and stalk phenotypes that guide the formation of new blood vessels.
I developed a mechanistic, ordinary differential equation-based model to investigate how endothelial cells communicate and differentiate under different oxygen conditions and levels of VEGFA stimulation.
The model integrates intracellular and intercellular signaling to connect molecular pathway activation with endothelial cell patterning and functional responses.

title: Endothelial Patterning Through Notch–Dll4 Signaling
text:
Scientific question
How do oxygen availability, VEGFA gradients, and Notch–Dll4 signaling interact to regulate endothelial tip–stalk patterning during angiogenesis?
The work also investigated whether these mechanisms influence downstream endothelial functions, including nitric oxide production and vascular permeability.

title: Endothelial Patterning Through Notch–Dll4 Signaling
text:
Modeling approach
The model represents two neighboring endothelial cells that receive different levels of VEGFA stimulation and communicate through the Notch–Dll4 pathway.
It integrates six major signaling modules:

VEGF–VEGFR signaling
Notch–Dll4 lateral inhibition
HIF-mediated oxygen sensing
Akt–eNOS signaling
Raf–MEK–ERK signaling
Calcium and nitric oxide dynamics

The complete model contains:

183 molecular species
222 biochemical reactions
184 parameters
183 ordinary differential equations

Model development followed a structured workflow combining:

structural and practical identifiability analysis;
global sensitivity analysis;
parameter estimation using experimental time-course data;
uncertainty quantification through bootstrap analysis;
validation against independent experimental datasets.

To quantify endothelial phenotype, I introduced the Endothelial Cell Pattern Index (ECPI), a dimensionless ratio based on molecular markers associated with stalk and tip cells:
\[
\mathrm{ECPI} =
\frac{[\mathrm{Hes1}]\,[\mathrm{VEGFR1}]}
     {[\mathrm{Dll4}]\,[\mathrm{VEGFR2}]}
\]
Higher values indicate a stronger stalk-like signaling profile relative to a tip-like profile.

title: Endothelial Patterning Through Notch–Dll4 Signaling
text:
Key findings

Endothelial patterning requires differential VEGFA stimulation
The model predicted that neighboring endothelial cells require unequal exposure to extracellular VEGFA to establish distinct tip and stalk signaling profiles.
Hypoxia increased the activation of several angiogenic pathways but did not independently generate cell patterning when both cells received equivalent VEGFA stimulation.


Patterning mechanisms depend on oxygen and time
The signaling mechanisms controlling tip–stalk differentiation differed between normoxia and hypoxia. Their relative influence also changed with the duration of hypoxic exposure.
These results indicate that both oxygen availability and time under hypoxia should be considered when attempting to control endothelial phenotype.


Multiple pathways shape tip–stalk identity
Although Notch signaling directly mediates lateral inhibition, global sensitivity analysis showed that VEGF, ERK, and Akt signaling parameters also strongly influenced the endothelial patterning index.
This illustrates how cell fate emerges from the integrated signaling network rather than from the Notch pathway in isolation.


Notch signaling may influence vascular permeability
Simulations predicted that changes in Dll4-mediated Notch activation produce different nitric oxide responses in neighboring endothelial cells.
Because VEGF-induced nitric oxide contributes to vascular hyperpermeability, the model suggests a potential mechanistic connection between Notch signaling and vascular leakiness.


The model reproduced experimental Notch inhibition
Simulated inhibition of γ-secretase with DAPT reduced VEGF-induced NICD and Hes1 signaling. Consequently, the two endothelial cells developed more similar molecular profiles, consistent with published experimental observations.

title: Endothelial Patterning Through Notch–Dll4 Signaling
Endothelial Patterning Through Notch–Dll4 Signaling
Endothelial Patterning Through Notch–Dll4 Signaling
text:
Scientific value
This project provides an integrative computational framework for studying how molecular signaling coordinates endothelial behavior during angiogenesis.
The model can be extended to investigate interventions targeting Notch, VEGF, or related pathways in pro- and anti-angiogenic therapeutic contexts. It also established the methodological foundation for my subsequent mechanistic models of HGF–VEGF signaling and HIF pathway regulation.

title: Mechanistic Modeling of HGF-VEGF Signaling
text:
Hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) are major regulators of angiogenesis. Although both can promote endothelial proliferation, they can have contrasting effects on vascular permeability and vessel stability.
This project developed an integrative mechanistic model to investigate how HGF and VEGF separately and jointly regulate endothelial-cell proliferation and permeability under normoxia and hypoxia.



Application: angiogenesis and vascular signaling
Model type: mechanistic ordinary differential equation model
Scale: 93 species, 112 reactions, and 186 parameters
Calibration: global parameter estimation with identifiability-based parameter selection
Evaluation: sensitivity analysis, bootstrap uncertainty quantification, residual analysis, and independent validation
Software: MATLAB and SimBiology
Publication: iScience, 2025

title: Mechanistic Modeling of HGF-VEGF Signaling
text:
Scientific questions
The model was designed to investigate:

Which mechanisms may explain the divergent effects of HGF and VEGF on vascular permeability?
How does acute hypoxia alter signaling through these pathways?
Does HGF require VEGFR2 activation to influence proliferation or permeability?
How might HGF and VEGF be combined to promote proliferation while maintaining vascular stability?

title: Mechanistic Modeling of HGF-VEGF Signaling
Mechanistic Modeling of HGF-VEGF Signaling
text:
Key findings

HGF and VEGF produce distinct permeability responses
Dose-response simulations predicted that HGF can counteract VEGF-induced endothelial permeability. However, increasing VEGF exposure progressively reduced the ability of HGF to maintain vascular stability.


HGF does not require VEGFR2 activation
The model predicted that HGF can influence endothelial proliferation and permeability through cMet-mediated signaling without requiring VEGFR2 activation.


PAK1 provides a mechanistic explanation
Site-specific PAK1 phosphorylation emerged as an important mechanism distinguishing HGF- and VEGF-mediated permeability responses.


Context-specific pathway regulation
Global sensitivity analyses showed that the parameters governing proliferation and permeability depend on ligand exposure, oxygen conditions, and the timing of the response.

title: About
text:
I am a Brazilian biomedical engineer and computational scientist with a PhD in Biomedical Engineering from Johns Hopkins University. I am currently a postdoctoral fellow at the Popel Systems Biology Lab (Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine), where I develop mechanistic models to support translational research and drug development.
My work lies at the intersection of biology, pharmacology, and computation. I use mathematical models to organize complex biological knowledge, test mechanistic hypotheses, quantify uncertainty, identify biomarkers and investigate how differences between individuals may influence treatment response.

title: About
text:
My research path
My research began in mechanistic systems biology, with models of signaling and regulatory processes involving Notch-Dll4, hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), and hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF). These projects taught me how to translate biological mechanisms into mathematical structures and how to use models to generate experimentally relevant insight.
I subsequently expanded into quantitative systems pharmacology, oncology, and virtual-population modeling. This work focuses on connecting drug mechanisms and biological heterogeneity with clinically relevant outcomes.
I am now building additional expertise in pharmacometrics, including noncompartmental analysis, population pharmacokinetics, covariate modeling, model diagnostics, simulation, and uncertainty quantification.

title: About
About
text:
Emerging directions
A long-term goal of my work is to apply quantitative pharmacology and systems modeling to a broader range of therapeutic questions. I am particularly interested in natural products, medicinal plants, and complex interventions that are difficult to investigate using conventional single-target approaches.
This direction brings together my background in mechanistic modeling with my growing experience in pharmacometrics and translational pharmacology.

title: Mechanistic Modeling of HIF Signaling
text:
Hypoxia activates cellular oxygen-sensing mechanisms that promote adaptation, survival, and angiogenesis. Although HIF1 and HIF2 are both central to this response, they exhibit different temporal behaviors and regulatory roles that are difficult to resolve experimentally.
This project developed a mechanistic model of the PHD-HIF-VEGFA signaling axis in endothelial cells, with explicit representation of HIF1α, HIF2α, PHD2, PHD3, and VEGFA mRNA.



Application: endothelial hypoxia signaling
Model type: mechanistic ordinary differential equation model
Calibration: particle swarm optimization followed by local refinement
Evaluation: identifiability analysis, uncertainty quantification, residual analysis, and independent validation
Software: MATLAB and SimBiology
Publication: iScience, 2026

title: Mechanistic Modeling of HIF Signaling
Mechanistic Modeling of HIF Signaling
Mechanistic Modeling of HIF Signaling
text:
Key findings

Time-dependent HIF isoform switch
The model reproduced a rapid HIF1α response after the onset of hypoxia, followed by a delayed and more sustained HIF2α response. This captured the experimentally reported transition from acute HIF1-dominated signaling to prolonged HIF2-dominated signaling.


Oxygen-dependent response
Simulations predicted graded stabilization of HIF1α and HIF2α across oxygen levels, accompanied by dose- and time-dependent induction of VEGFA mRNA.


Distinct roles of PHD2 and PHD3
Perturbation simulations predicted that PHD2 and PHD3 have complementary, non-redundant, and isoform-specific effects on HIF stabilization and VEGFA regulation.


Fractional regulation of VEGFA
The model quantified the changing contributions of HIF1 and HIF2 to VEGFA mRNA regulation during prolonged hypoxia.

title: Mechanistic Modeling of HIF Signaling
text:
Model evaluation
The model was calibrated using endothelial-cell experimental data and validated against independent datasets not used for parameter estimation.
Across validation observables:

Pearson correlations ranged from 0.70 to 0.95;
Runs tests showed no systematic residual bias (p ≥ 0.35);
the model reproduced the major temporal trends of HIF1α, HIF2α, and VEGFA mRNA.

The analysis also documented limitations arising from heterogeneous experimental datasets, measurement platforms, and oxygen conditions.

I co-developed the study concept, constructed the complete computational model, performed all simulations and quantitative analyses, and wrote the initial manuscript draft.

The model provides a technically evaluated and reusable representation of endothelial hypoxia signaling. It can serve as a module for larger models of ischemic disease, angiogenesis, tumor hypoxia, and quantitative systems pharmacology.

title: Quantitative Systems Pharmacology in Oncology
text:
NotePublic-project scope



This page describes the scientific scope and modeling methods involved in my current postdoctoral research.
Because the work is ongoing and conducted within an academic–industry collaboration, compound identities, model structure, parameter values, simulation results, and project-specific conclusions are not presented publicly at this stage.

title: Quantitative Systems Pharmacology in Oncology
text:
Project overview
My current postdoctoral research applies quantitative systems pharmacology to translational questions in oncology drug development.
The work uses mechanistic computational models to connect drug mechanisms, tumor biology, immune response, biological heterogeneity, and clinical outcomes. The broader objective is to investigate how these interacting processes may shape differences in treatment response across patients and patient subgroups.
Unlike empirical models that primarily describe associations in observed data, QSP models explicitly represent biological mechanisms and their interactions. This allows them to be used for hypothesis generation, simulation of alternative treatment scenarios, and investigation of the biological factors associated with response variability.

title: Quantitative Systems Pharmacology in Oncology
text:
Scientific focus
The research addresses questions such as:

How do drug mechanisms interact with the tumor microenvironment?
Which biological differences may contribute to heterogeneous treatment responses?
Can virtual populations reproduce clinically relevant variability?
How robust are model predictions to alternative population selections and parameter assumptions?
Which model components or biomarkers are most strongly associated with simulated treatment outcomes?
How can preclinical, mechanistic, and clinical evidence be integrated within a consistent quantitative framework?

title: Quantitative Systems Pharmacology in Oncology
text:
Modeling approach
The project combines several modeling components:

Mechanistic model development
Biological processes and therapeutic mechanisms are represented through systems of ordinary differential equations and mechanistic reaction networks.
Model development includes evaluating assumptions, parameterization, initialization, numerical stability, and the relationships between model components.


Virtual populations
Virtual individuals are generated by varying selected biological and pharmacological parameters within plausible ranges.
Candidate individuals are evaluated against biological and clinical constraints, and subsets are selected to reproduce relevant population characteristics.
Because more than one virtual population may satisfy the same calibration criteria, I also investigate robustness across alternative population selections.


In silico clinical trials
Selected virtual populations are simulated under alternative treatment conditions using clinically relevant dosing and assessment schedules.
The simulated outcomes can then be compared with population-level clinical evidence and evaluated across relevant biological subgroups.


Biomarker and sensitivity analyses
Sensitivity and feature analyses are used to investigate which parameters, baseline characteristics, and longitudinal biological responses are associated with simulated therapeutic outcomes.
These analyses support mechanistic interpretation and help identify hypotheses for further experimental or clinical investigation.

title: Quantitative Systems Pharmacology in Oncology
Quantitative Systems Pharmacology in Oncology
text:
Computational workflow
The project requires an iterative workflow connecting biological reasoning, computational implementation, and model evaluation:

Define the translational question.
Review the relevant biological and clinical evidence.
Translate mechanisms into mathematical representations.
Evaluate model behavior and numerical stability.
Generate biologically plausible virtual individuals.
Select and qualify virtual populations.
Simulate treatment and clinical-assessment scenarios.
Compare predictions with available evidence.
Evaluate robustness and uncertainty.
Interpret the results in the context of model assumptions and limitations.

title: Quantitative Systems Pharmacology in Oncology
Quantitative Systems Pharmacology in Oncology
text:
Broader relevance
QSP provides a framework for integrating evidence that would otherwise remain distributed across experimental studies, clinical trials, and biological literature.
Its value is not limited to predicting a single outcome. It can also make assumptions explicit, reveal gaps in available evidence, test mechanistic hypotheses, and help prioritize questions for further investigation.

title: Projects
text:
Quantitative Systems Pharmacology
Projects using mechanistic models and virtual populations to connect drug mechanisms, biological heterogeneity, and treatment response.

Oncology drug development
My current postdoctoral research applies quantitative systems pharmacology to questions in oncology drug development. This work integrates therapeutic mechanisms, tumor biology, immune response, and biological heterogeneity within mechanistic computational models.
My contributions include model development, virtual-population generation, in silico clinical-trial simulation, treatment-response analysis, and investigation of potential biomarkers.
Because this work is part of an ongoing academic–industry collaboration, project-specific models, compounds, results, and implementation details are not presented publicly at this stage.

Natural Products and Translational Modeling
Quantitative approaches for natural products, medicinal plants, and complex biological interventions.

Medicinal plants as an emerging research direction
I am developing a research direction that connects medicinal plants and natural products with quantitative pharmacology, systems biology, and translational modeling.
Initial work focuses on organizing evidence linking medicinal plants, bioactive compounds, molecular targets, biological pathways, and disease contexts. The longer-term goal is to identify questions for which mechanistic modeling can help integrate fragmented experimental evidence and prioritize testable therapeutic hypotheses.
This area is presented as an emerging direction rather than as a completed research program. Public case studies will be added as the underlying datasets, research questions, and modeling workflows mature.
